comments.text:
Security features like this works, until it doesn't.
When I installed WireGuard on macOS, I was happy to discover that it stores private keys in the system keychain. Accessing the private key requires Touch ID.
Then one day after a system upgrade, the WireGuard app crashed on startup with:
[APP] Unable to open config from keychain: -25300
Then the app deleted all profiles because they are all "orphaned", apparently for "keychain consistency" [0].
From then on, I just use a text editor to edit my WireGuard configuration files, and import them to the app. The bug still exists to this day [1].

comments.author: mavam
comments.text:
One fundamental problem with agentic development is that accessing the secure enclave key requires human presence. If you're running headless and aren't logged in, Secretive (not sure about others) will not be able to access the enclave, even when you only chose "notify" and not "touchid".
This is why I'm skeptical that the approach can scale reliably, even though I'm relying on it today. (Yes, PATs would fix this, but the enclave model is what I'm trying to retain for now.) What I've done instead is wrote a small daemon that sets the SSH authentication socket and does agent forwarding. This works when I'm traveling with laptop...but not yet from my mobile phone.
Example:
Laptop                                   Remote Mac
┌─────────────────────┐                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
│ Secretive           │                  │ ssh / git commit -S      │
│ (Secure Enclave)    │                  │          │               │
│        ▲            │  ForwardAgent    │          ▼               │
│        └── ssh ─────┼─────────────────►│  ~/.ssh/agent.sock       │
│                     │                  │  (stable proxy)          │
└─────────────────────┘                  │

comments.author: jen729w
comments.text:
I use 1Password's `op` for this, but with an allowance: my dev environment keys.
I found I was getting fingerprint fatigue. Do I need a fingerprint request
every
time my dev server wants to connect to dev Supabase? No. That's expected, and zero risk. There's no data there.
I worried that a nefarious request would be auto-approved by me. When you see 20 requests a day, your muscle memory just reaches for the sensor.
So I have a separate 1Password vault that a service account [0] can read. That token is in my environment as OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN, which the `op` tool understands.
It also has access to a vault with 'AI-safe' keys that I want Claude to be able to access without asking me.
Now, these requests work invisibly. And when I see a fingerprint popup, it's unusual, and I don't auto-approve by habit.
I also keep an item called '_One-day keys' in a separate vault. (The underscore just pushing it to the top of the list for easy access.)
It has prod keys, mostly restricted read-only. If required, I move that over to the open vault. Claude knows this item and has instructions to remind me to move it back out when it's finished what it was doing.
[0]:
https://www.1password.dev/serv

stories.title_en: A great old-timey game-programming hack (2013)

comments.author: sehugg
comments.text:
The 6502 has a more narrow and diabolical version of the 6809's PSHS trick. The BRK instruction pushes the PC and status register to the stack in three consecutive cycles, and is pretty much the only non-interrupt instruction that writes more than twice.
The Atari 2600 has horizontal object counters that you can't set directly, but they latch when you write to them, and they set the corresponding object to the X position of the beam at that cycle. Pole Position requires three of these objects to draw the left/right side of the road and center line, and they are supposed to meet at the horizon.
But the beam moves to the right 3 pixels for every CPU cycle, and writing with STA would result in each being separated by 9 pixels. What's the fix? Move the stack pointer to where the object pointers live (the 2600 maps the stack to zero page, where the RAM and registers live) and invoke BRK, making sure the BRK vector returns you to the next instruction. The object pointers are adjacent, so BRK writes to each object pointer on successive cycles, and now each of them is 1 cycle = 3 pixels apart.

They had a file informally maintained that listed every single product they had for sale, in a format that could be read on a PC. He was really good at searching it with his text editor, but he wanted a MS-DOS based stand alone program to make it easy to search for his co-workers. Thus was born, PCxREF which was a Turbo Pascal based program I wrote, that included search.
My first pass at it was a naïve search using the built in string matching. Because of the size of the file, and the speed of PCs, it would sometimes take more than 30 seconds to do a search.  Ward wanted it faster,
much

> Years ago, I was working at Video Seven, a now-vanished video adapter manufacturer, helping to develop a VGA clone. The fellow who was designing Video Seven’s VGA chip, Tom Wilson, had worked around the clock for months to make his VGA run as fast as possible, and was confident he had pretty much maxed out its performance. As Tom was putting the finishing touches on his chip design, however, news came fourth-hand that a competitor, Paradise, had juiced up the performance of the clone they were developing by putting in a FIFO.
> That was all he knew; there was no information about what sort of FIFO, or how much it helped, or anything else. Something seems wrong here.  They took a non-trivial piece of human-written code that has had bugs in the past, formally verified the whole library, and found zero bugs?
I can believe that it's possible to get the LLM to write proofs, but I can't believe there were zero bugs in the system they verified.  I wonder if they got the theorems wrong, or if they only proved narrow properties of the system.
I've had Claude formally verify crypto and data storage formats.  It wrote theorems that looked fine and the formal verification passed but the resulting code contained many, many bugs that other implementations of the same things found with ad hoc testing.
The way the announcement is written, we should expect zero bugs in libsignal moving forward, and I guess time will tell whether that happens or not.

1. AI Lean is not perfect and AI can easily cheat given it is writing the lean. For anyone playing around with AI Lean code at minimum you need another adversarial prompt to review the ai generated lean.
2. In the paper poking around I see they did re-introduce some bugs to verify it would catch them, but they didn't find any bugs it looks like.  Maybe signal is just amazing with many eyes reviewing it, but the real story for the rest of us is that if you start AI converting to Lean the value will be in what assumptions it finds. Even for stuff I thought was really logically tight, Lean found a few minor things I had to fix. Similar to fuzzing where I have never not found bugs when I introduced fuzzing into a codebase I expect the same for converting specs to lean.

I was very impressed, until I squinted a little. It had implemented the whole thing backwards, in a way which was not only pointless (didn't achieve any of the stated goals) but actually made things worse than before!

comments.author: basilgohar

I think looking at AI usage for code and development from an engineering perspective is going to be an exercise in frustration. I'm a software engineer for 20+ years and I've pivoted to using AI for my code 100%. I find it invaluable about the only way to stay relevant and run a business nowadays. Happy for anyone to disagree with me, because I don't
want
to be right for the first time in my life.
That said, my experience tells me that enterprise and business coding has rarely ever been about stable or robust codebases. We engineers and a fraction of competent engineering managers and a vanishing small number of directors fought against business interests to ensure quality was priority when it came to code, but it was always an uphill battle and we were oftentimes disciplined for spending too much time on quality and design.
A timed cadence of release is anathema to quality code because you can't timebox it.
So, AI is just the extension of that. Do I try to ensure my agents design code I would consider to be good? Yes, absolutely! But I've fully outsourced it and I find it's also fully capable of fixing it's own mistakes. I've gone far beyond anything I individually or even with a

comments.author: iagooar
comments.text:
This reads like a piece of content written a year ago. Things have radically changed since then.
"AI writes shallow tests" - used to be true, not true anymore since Astra and Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5.
"AI writes overly complex ccode" - only if you let it. A "do not overengineer it" or "Pareto, 80% result with 20% of effort" go a long long way.
"Reliance on AI decreases human understanding" - human understanding does not decrease, it just moves up a level or two. The same way you do not really understand how the Linux kernel works, nor do you know how assembly really works (with probably a bunch of exceptions here given this is the HN crowd!). And then there is hardware and physics too.
Understanding code, algorithms and data structures becomes a rarer need than it used to be.
"AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar" - if you are stuck with the mantra that humans must review the code today, then obviously that statement becomes true. The problem is the assumption, not the observation. The good news about AI progressing fast is that coding AND reviewing get better and better with each release.
I know it is tough to let go. But as a software engineer, the sooner you do it, th

comments.author: momojo
comments.text: The term "injection molded coding" has been bouncing around my head lately. I empathize and have personally experienced the fragility and opaqueness the OP describes. But I wonder if we're like master carpenters, grieving as we inspect a warm plastic chair leg, fresh from the injection mold, wondering what the future of furniture making will look like when each chair leg is mass-produced, and not lovingly carved by hand.

comments.author: monjerry
comments.text: Code quality is not an issue.....until it is. Everyone will be happy if things seem to be working and moving fast, it's only until you start seeing symptoms like not being able to change things without breaking existing features or even seeing an increase in tokens burned for reading complex code bases that you will start caring about code quality (which i imagine now people will just have AI try to fix it's own mess).

comments.author: peterbell_nyc
comments.text:
I'm not sure that "AI generates..." articles are going to age well.
My immediate question would be what kind of adversarial reviews and deterministic gates did the author write to capture the dimensions of maintainability (lack of DRY, cyclomatic complexity, unclear naming, poorly architected flows, etc) that they cared about.
Don't get me wrong. When I was speeding along at 200 PRs a day (personal projects - I would not have inflicted them on others) I pretty quickly slopped together a big ball of mud, but as I'm re-generating my estate (a) the models are a little better but (b) I'm adding a lot more rigor around verification (correctness, performance, security, operational costs and maintainability). It's not an easy problem to solve, but it feels to me like an engineering endeavor, not speculative rocket science.
I fully understand that many AI generated code bases do indeed suffer from more incidents and less maintainability, but I think it's important to distinguish between what is common and what is possible as the fix for one is improving the rigor of your verification whereas the fix for the other would be either accepting crappy code or giving up on LLMs.

comments.author: jasode
comments.text:
I don't disagree with the article but it may give some readers the impression that pre-AI hand-written code wasn't fragile.
Here's the famous commentary about Oracle RDBMS codebase of 25 million lines:
https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18442941
Every big company codebase with millions of lines devolves into a similar state.  The small codebase starts with clean conceptual integrity.  It then inevitably decays into incomprehensible spaghetti code as more people are added to it.  Various reasons for it including the later devs caring less about the code than the initial team of devs, deadlines, avoiding refactoring because of fear about breaking things, etc.
If you don't want AI to create fragile code, you have to apply the same quality gates that would have been applied to pre-AI hand-written code to keep everything clean.  Most companies don't do that.

comments.author: yodsanklai
comments.text:
I don't think this matters anymore. Software is becoming a black box and agents make it works, as long as you can provide some reasonable spec of what you want to do, and a bit of supervising and directions.
Right now, they're not great at following good software engineering principles. They do the job, with verbose code, lots of duplication, abstraction leaks, useless unit tests and so on.
Is it an issue? you could think that in the long term it'll be, that AI won't be able to handle the complexity it introduced, but I'm not really worried about it. Most software isn't that big, and agents are getting better by the day. And if you really care about design, it's not too hard to instruct your agent to follow your standards.
I wish it wasn't the case and that I could justify my experience and expertise for a few more years, but the facts are there.

Programming is about engaging with high level mathematical abstractions.
To the extent AI can do this high level thinking, it is going to be able to do absolutely everything else humans can. Programming (when not underestimated) is as hard as the hardest cognitive task humans can do.

comments.author: Animats
comments.text:
This is a "build it and they will come" project.
It's not a "we put the inner loop of ML entirely in hardware" project. That would make more sense technically. You could cram a lot of little independent neural net inference units on one chip. But if it was pitched that way, the questions would be "Why isn't NVidia doing this", and "After you do it, what keeps NVidia from doing it". There are lots of people pitching "AI chips", with modest success.
The history of general-purpose massively parallel machines isn't good. From the Illiac IV to the Playstation 3, there's been dud after dud in this space. You can build them, but the users don't come. This sort of architecture is great if you have some specific problem that parallelizes, such as finite-element analysis or neural networks.
(I've used an NCube, and I kind of liked the Transputer concept. But both were dead ends.)
